levels.title: The Big Picture
levels.subtitle: World economy: concept, history, structure, country groups
briefing: The world economy is a system of national economies linked by the international division of labour.
The world market (exchange) appeared first, in the 16th–18th centuries; the world economy took shape by the end of the 19th century.
World output was about $115 trillion in 2025; growth 3.5% (IMF). The US (~26%) and China (~17%) produce over 40% of it.
Size (potential) = total GDP, population, resources. Level of development = GDP per capita, HDI, productivity, share of services.
Main groups: advanced economies, developing countries, economies in transition, NICs, least developed countries.

levels.title: Trade Winds
levels.subtitle: International trade: factors, division of labour, indicators, policy
briefing: Factors of production: land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship; today also technology, knowledge and data.
Comparative advantage (Ricardo): specialize where your relative cost is lowest. Heckscher–Ohlin: export goods that use your abundant factor.
Forms of IDL: general → particular → single (detailed); today global value chains.
Key indicators: X − M (balance), X + M (turnover), X/GDP (export quota), export prices ÷ import prices × 100 (terms of trade).
World trade in goods and services passed $35 trillion in 2025; top goods exporters: China, US, Germany.
Trade policy tools: tariffs (ad valorem, specific) and non-tariff measures (quotas, licences, standards, subsidies).

levels.title: Know-How
levels.subtitle: Technology exchange, life cycle, transfer, licences
briefing: Embodied technology comes inside machines; disembodied technology is knowledge: patents, licences, know-how.
Commercial forms of exchange are paid (licences, engineering, franchising); non-commercial are free (publications, conferences, academic exchange).
Technology life cycle: emergence → introduction → growth → maturity → decline. A licence is most expensive at the growth stage.
The largest channel of technology transfer is inside multinational enterprises.
Licences: simple (non-exclusive), exclusive, full; payments: royalties, lump sum or combined.
Global Innovation Index 2026: Switzerland, Sweden, US, South Korea, Singapore lead; China is 10th.

levels.title: Follow the Capital
levels.subtitle: Investment, FDI and portfolio flows
briefing: Global FDI rose 6% to about $1.6 trillion in 2025; the US was both the largest recipient ($277 bn) and the largest source.
FDI = 10% or more of voting power (lasting interest and control); below 10% = portfolio investment.
Dunning's motives: market-seeking, resource-seeking, efficiency-seeking, strategic-asset-seeking.
Entry modes: greenfield (new plant) vs brownfield (mergers and acquisitions).
FDI comes in waves that start with technology and liberalization and end with crises.
Portfolio capital is "hot money": it grows with low rates abroad and flees during crises.

levels.title: Money Matters
levels.subtitle: World finance and monetary systems
briefing: Finance globalized through liberalization, ICT, floating exchange rates and financial innovation.
The FX market turns over $9.6 trillion a day (BIS, 2025); London handles about 38% of it.
Gold standard (to 1914, restored until the 1930s): fixed gold content, free convertibility, free gold flows.
Bretton Woods (1944): $35 per ounce, currencies pegged to the dollar ±1%; ended in 1971–1973 (Triffin dilemma).
Jamaican system (1976): gold demonetized, free choice of exchange-rate regime; the dollar still holds about 57% of reserves.
EMS (1979): ECU + ERM; EMU: euro from 1999; 21 members since Bulgaria joined in 2026.

levels.title: Giants Without Borders
levels.subtitle: Transnational corporations and Dunning's OLI paradigm
briefing: MNEs produce about one-third of world GDP and more than half of world exports (OECD).
Transnationality Index (UNCTAD) = average of foreign shares in assets, sales and employment.
Dunning's OLI: Ownership (what the firm has), Location (where to produce), Internalization (how to use the advantage).
O only → licensing; O + I → export; O + I + L → FDI.
Modern features: value chains, non-equity modes, digital "asset-light" MNEs, MNEs from emerging markets, friendshoring.
Strategic alliances keep firms legally independent; mergers and acquisitions do not.

levels.title: Boom & Bust
levels.subtitle: Business cycles, recessions, unemployment, inflation
briefing: Phases: expansion → peak → contraction (recession) → trough → recovery.
Cycles: Kitchin 3–4 years (inventories), Juglar 7–11 (equipment), Kuznets 15–25 (construction), Kondratiev 45–60 (technology).
Global recessions (World Bank): 1975, 1982, 1991, 2009, 2020; 2001 was a global slowdown.
1974–75 oil embargo and stagflation; 1980–82 second oil shock + Volcker; 1991–93 unsynchronized; 2001–03 dot-com crash.
Okun's law: each 1 p.p. of cyclical unemployment ≈ 2–2.5% of lost output.
Inflation: demand-pull vs cost-push; CPI (Laspeyres) vs GDP deflator (Paasche).

levels.title: One Planet
levels.subtitle: Globalization, integration, global problems, competitiveness
briefing: Global transformation: national economies turn into one integrated system — and now fragment again into blocs.
Interdependence spreads shocks: 2008 crisis, 2021 chip shortage, 2026 Middle East energy shock.
Balassa's stages: FTA → customs union → common market → economic and monetary union → full integration.
Global problems: war and peace, North–South gap, climate, resources, demography, pandemics, digital and AI risks.
2024 was the first calendar year more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels (WMO).
Competitiveness = productivity (Porter's diamond). IMD 2026: Singapore, Hong Kong, Switzerland lead.

levels.title: North America
levels.subtitle: USA and Canada
briefing: The US produces about 26% of world GDP ($30.8 trn in 2025); consumption is about 68% of GDP, services about 80%.
Factors: resources (shale oil and gas), immigration, deep capital markets, the dollar, technology, institutions.
Problems: deficit of $2.0 trn (6.2% of GDP) in FY2026, public debt at 100% of GDP, record goods trade deficit.
2025 trade: exports $3.43 trn, imports $4.33 trn, deficit $901.5 bn; services surplus $339.5 bn.
Canada: resource-rich G7 economy; 71.6% of goods exports go to the US; GDP +1.7% in 2025.
CUSMA: the US declined to renew it on 1 July 2026 — annual reviews until expiry in 2036.

levels.title: Rising Sun
levels.subtitle: Japan
briefing: Japan's GDP is about $4.2 trn; India overtook it in 2025, so it is now 4th–5th in the world.
Almost no natural resources; strengths: cars, robotics, machine tools, chip-making equipment and materials.
Post-war stages: occupation → "miracle" (~10% growth) → oil shocks → bubble → "lost decades" → Abenomics → inflation returns.
Ageing: nearly 30% of people are 65+; public debt is the highest among developed countries.
Bank of Japan raised its rate to 0.75% in December 2025 — a 30-year high; GDP +1.1% in 2025.
Trade strategy: CPTPP, RCEP, EPA with the EU; production networks across Asia and the US.

levels.title: Core Europe
levels.subtitle: Germany and France
briefing: Germany: 3rd economy in the world (~$5 trn); GDP −0.9% (2023), −0.5% (2024), +0.2% (2025).
German strengths: Mittelstand SMEs, dual vocational training, engineering, exports of about 40% of GDP.
German problems: expensive energy after 2022, car industry under pressure, ageing; 2025 reform of the debt brake + €500 bn fund.
France: about 7th in the world, 2nd in the euro area; aerospace, luxury, nuclear energy, tourism, agriculture.
French model: strong state ("dirigisme"), very high public spending; deficit 5.1% and debt 115.6% of GDP (2025).
Germany and France are the "engine" of European integration.

levels.title: Islands & Peninsula
levels.subtitle: United Kingdom and Italy
briefing: UK: about 6th in the world; services ~80% of the economy; London is a top financial centre (38% of FX trading).
Brexit: left the EU on 31 January 2020; trade under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement since 2021; joined CPTPP in 2024.
UK growth: 1.1% (2024) → 1.3–1.4% (2025); weak productivity since 2008; surplus in services, deficit in goods.
Italy: euro area's 3rd economy, EU's 2nd manufacturer; SME industrial districts; North–South divide.
Italy 2025: GDP +0.5%, deficit 3.1%, debt about 137% of GDP; largest beneficiary of NextGenerationEU.
Italian state: IRI history, "golden power" over foreign takeovers, Mattei Plan for Africa, exit from the Belt and Road (2023).

levels.title: Asian Dragons
levels.subtitle: China and newly industrialized countries
briefing: China: 2nd economy (140.2 trn yuan ≈ $20 trn, +5.0% in 2025), largest manufacturer and exporter, trade surplus $1.19 trn.
Reforms since 1978 (Deng Xiaoping): gradual, experimental — household responsibility, SEZs, WTO entry in 2001.
Problems: property crisis, local debt, weak consumption, deflation pressure, shrinking population.
15th Five-Year Plan (2026–2030): technological self-reliance, "new quality productive forces"; 2026 target 4.5–5%.
Asian tigers: South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore — export-led growth, developmental state, education.
AI boom: Taiwan grew 8.63% in 2025 (fastest in 15 years); South Korea about 1.0%.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the world MARKET and the world ECONOMY?
questions.explanation: The world market (16th–18th c.) is the sphere of exchange based on the international division of labour. The world economy (formed by the end of the 19th c.) is the wider system: production + exchange + distribution + consumption.

options.text: The world market covers only exchange; the world economy also includes production, distribution and consumption
The world market includes services, while the world economy includes only goods
The world market is regulated by the WTO, while the world economy has no regulation
The world economy appeared first, in the 15th century, and the world market grew out of it only in the 20th century

questions.question: What links national economies into one world economy?
questions.explanation: Countries specialize and exchange — that is the international division of labour (IDL). It creates flows of goods, services, capital, labour and technology between them.

options.text: A single world currency issued by the IMF
Equal levels of economic development everywhere
A common world government with binding laws

questions.question: Which of these are SUBJECTS (actors) of the world economy? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Subjects are actors that make decisions: MNEs, states, international organisations, regional blocs, banks, households. The division of labour is the basis of the world economy, and gold reserves are an instrument — neither is an actor.

options.text: International organisations such as the IMF and WTO

questions.question: Put the stages of the world economy in chronological order.
questions.explanation: 16th–18th c. preconditions → late 18th–19th c. industrial revolution → 1945–1991 bipolar world (IMF, World Bank, GATT) → 1990s–2000s globalization (WTO 1995, China in the WTO 2001).

options.text: The WTO and China's entry drive globalization
Bretton Woods institutions shape a bipolar post-war economy
Great Geographical Discoveries create the first world market
Industrial Revolution makes Britain the "workshop of the world"

questions.question: Which period is often called the "first globalization"?
questions.explanation: Between the 1870s and WWI the gold standard, capital exports, railways and steamships created a highly integrated world economy. WWI and the Great Depression then broke it apart.

questions.question: What characterised the world economy in 1914–1945?
questions.explanation: Two world wars and the 1929–1933 Depression led to high tariffs, competitive devaluations and closed currency blocs. GATT and liberalization came only after 1945.

options.text: Record growth of world trade driven by global value chains of MNEs
Rapid trade liberalization under GATT and fixed exchange rates under Bretton Woods
Disintegration: wars, the Great Depression, protectionism and currency blocs
Creation of a European single market and a common European currency

questions.question: Which term describes the period after the 2008 crisis, when world trade stopped growing faster than world GDP?
questions.explanation: "Hyperglobalization" (1990s–2008) meant trade grew much faster than GDP. After 2008 the trade-to-GDP ratio flattened — "slowbalization". Since 2018 tariffs and conflicts add fragmentation.

questions.question: According to the IMF (October 2026), how fast did the world economy grow in 2025?
questions.explanation: World growth was 3.5% in 2025; the IMF expected it to slow to 3.1% in 2026 because of the Middle East energy shock. World output was about $115 trillion.

questions.question: Which two economies together produce more than 40% of world output (nominal GDP)?
questions.explanation: The US (~$30.8 trn, about 26%) and China (~$20 trn, about 17%) together exceed 40% of world GDP (~$115 trn in 2025).

questions.question: In 2025, which country overtook Japan to become the world's 4th-largest economy?
questions.explanation: India's GDP (~$4.18 trn) passed Japan's in 2025 — a sign that the world's economic centre of gravity is moving to Asia. Germany is 3rd.

questions.question: Which indicator best shows a country's LEVEL of development rather than its economic SIZE?
questions.explanation: Size (economic potential) = total GDP, population, resources, exports. Level of development = per-person and quality measures: GDP/GNI per capita, HDI, productivity, share of services.

questions.question: Which dimensions make up the UN Human Development Index (HDI)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The HDI combines three dimensions: a long and healthy life, knowledge, and a decent standard of living. Economic structure and population size are not part of it.

questions.question: Under the World Bank FY2027 classification, a country with GNI per capita of $15,000 (Atlas method) is…
questions.explanation: FY2027 thresholds: low ≤ $1,175; lower-middle $1,176–4,635; upper-middle $4,636–14,375; high > $14,375. $15,000 is just above the high-income line. "Emerging-income" is not a World Bank group.

questions.question: China's GDP is about $20 trn, but GDP per person is only about $14,000. What does this tell us?
questions.explanation: Potential (size) and level (quality) are different things. A huge population makes the total large, but income per person is upper-middle — far below the US (~$90,000).

options.text: China's level of development is higher than that of the US because its total GDP grows faster
China is a least developed country
China has a huge economic potential but a middle level of development

questions.question: Which classification does the IMF use to divide countries?
questions.explanation: The IMF uses two big groups: about 40 advanced economies and the rest as EMDEs. Core/periphery comes from world-systems theory; "Three Worlds" is a Cold War term.

options.text: Core, semi-periphery and periphery economies by world-systems status
First, Second and Third World economies by political bloc
Advanced economies vs emerging market and developing economies
North, Centre and South economies by geographic location

questions.question: What are "countries with economies in transition"?
questions.explanation: The UN term covers post-socialist states (CIS, parts of South-East Europe) that went through market reforms after 1990.

options.text: Countries moving from agriculture to industry
Countries leaving the UN group of least developed countries after three reviews in a row
Former socialist countries moving from a planned to a market economy
Countries changing their currency to the euro

questions.question: Which statement about the least developed countries (LDCs) is correct?
questions.explanation: The UN Committee for Development Policy uses three criteria: GNI per capita, the Human Assets Index and the Economic Vulnerability Index. Most LDCs are in Africa.

options.text: A WTO list of developing members, updated every year according to their GDP growth rates
A list of all BRICS members and their closest trading partners
A UN list based on low income, weak human assets and economic vulnerability
An IMF list of all countries with a budget deficit above 3% of GDP

questions.question: Which grouping includes Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa plus newer members such as Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the UAE and Indonesia?
questions.explanation: BRICS expanded in 2024–2025. The G7 is a club of advanced economies, the OECD unites mostly developed countries, OPEC is an oil cartel.

questions.question: Which set lists the classical factors of production?
questions.explanation: Classical economists named land (natural resources), labour and capital; entrepreneurship was added later. Today knowledge, technology and data are also seen as factors.

questions.question: According to M. Porter, which of these is an ADVANCED factor rather than a basic one?
questions.explanation: Basic factors are inherited (resources, climate, unskilled labour). Advanced factors are created by investment — skills, R&D, digital infrastructure — and give lasting competitive advantage.

options.text: Large oil and natural gas deposits
Highly skilled engineers and research institutes
A warm climate with fertile farmland
Abundant cheap and unskilled labour moving from rural regions to cities

questions.question: The Heckscher–Ohlin theory says a country will export goods that…
questions.explanation: H–O: labour-abundant countries export labour-intensive goods, capital-abundant countries export capital-intensive goods. Absolute productivity is A. Smith's idea.

options.text: It produces with the highest absolute productivity compared with all its trading partners
Intensively use the factor of production it has in abundance

questions.question: What did the Leontief paradox show?
questions.explanation: In 1953 W. Leontief found that US exports used relatively more labour than imports — contrary to Heckscher–Ohlin. One explanation: American labour is highly skilled (human capital).

options.text: US exports were more labour-intensive than its imports, although the US was capital-abundant
Free trade lowered real wages in capital-abundant countries such as the US
Resource-rich countries grew more slowly than countries without natural resources
Trade between countries with similar factor endowments was close to zero in the post-war period

questions.question: Who formulated the theory of comparative advantage?
questions.explanation: Ricardo (1817): a country gains from trade by specializing where its relative (opportunity) cost is lowest, even if it is worse at producing everything. Smith's idea was absolute advantage.

questions.question: A country produces both wine and cloth less efficiently than its partner, but its disadvantage is smallest in wine. According to Ricardo, it should…
questions.explanation: Comparative advantage depends on relative costs. The country should specialize where its disadvantage is smallest (lowest opportunity cost) — then both partners gain.

options.text: Produce both goods and not trade
Specialize in cloth because its disadvantage there is larger
Specialize in wine and import cloth

questions.question: Order the forms of the international division of labour from the broadest to the most detailed.
questions.explanation: General IDL divides spheres, particular IDL divides products, single IDL divides parts and stages — the basis of global value chains.

options.text: Single (detailed) — between components and production stages
Particular — between types of finished products within an industry
General — between large spheres (industry vs agriculture)

questions.question: Germany exports cars to France and imports French cars. This is an example of…
questions.explanation: Intra-industry trade = exchange of similar products (cars for cars), typical for developed countries with similar factor endowments. Inter-industry trade = different products (oil for machines).

questions.question: A product makes up 10% of a country's exports but only 2% of world exports. What is its RCA (Balassa) index and what does it mean?
questions.explanation: RCA = share in the country's exports ÷ share in world exports = 10% ÷ 2% = 5. RCA above 1 indicates a revealed comparative advantage (specialization).

options.text: 5 — the country specializes in this product
0.2 — the country has no comparative advantage in this product

questions.question: Design in the US, chips from Taiwan, assembly in China or India. This is an example of…
questions.explanation: In global value chains production is split into stages located in different countries, usually coordinated by an MNE. It is the modern form of the detailed division of labour.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a segment of the world market?
questions.explanation: The world market includes markets of goods, services, capital, labour, technology and currencies. A national pension system belongs to domestic social policy.

questions.question: Put the stages of the world market's evolution in order.
questions.explanation: Exchange widened from local markets to regional trade, then to the world market (16th–18th c.), the mature world market of the 19th c., and finally today's global market.

options.text: Global market with the WTO and e-commerce
World market after the Great Geographical Discoveries
International market of neighbouring states (Middle Ages)

questions.question: How is the trade balance calculated?
questions.explanation: Trade balance = X − M (surplus if positive, deficit if negative). X + M is foreign trade turnover; X/GDP is the export quota.

questions.question: Germany exports about 40% of its GDP, the US about 11%. Which indicator is being compared?
questions.explanation: Export quota = X / GDP × 100%. It shows how open and export-dependent an economy is: Germany's model is export-led, the US relies on its huge domestic market.

questions.question: A country's export prices rose by 10% and its import prices by 21%. Its terms of trade index is about…
questions.explanation: ToT = export price index ÷ import price index × 100 = 110 ÷ 121 × 100 ≈ 91. Below 100 means each unit of exports now buys fewer imports.

questions.question: What does the foreign trade quota measure?
questions.explanation: Foreign trade quota = (X + M) / 2 / GDP × 100% (some textbooks use (X + M) / GDP). Don't confuse it with an import quota — a quantitative limit, which is a trade-policy tool.

options.text: A country's share in total world exports of goods and services
The openness of an economy — the share of foreign trade in GDP
The maximum amount of a good that may be imported in a year
The ratio of export prices to import prices in the base year

questions.question: What is the approximate split of world trade between goods and services?
questions.explanation: Goods still dominate, but services grow faster — about +9% in value in 2025 — driven by digitally delivered services.

options.text: About half goods and half services in value

questions.question: Which product group drove world trade growth in 2025?
questions.explanation: The AI investment boom pushed trade in semiconductors, servers and other electronics; UNCTAD and the WTO both named AI-related goods as the main driver.

options.text: Grain, fertilizers and other farm goods
Crude oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG)

questions.question: Which three countries were the largest goods exporters in 2025?
questions.explanation: China ($3.77 trn), the US ($2.19 trn) and Germany ($1.76 trn) gave about 29% of world goods exports together. The US is the largest importer.

questions.question: Which region gave about 71% of world merchandise trade volume growth in 2025 (WTO)?
questions.explanation: Asia is the largest and fastest-growing trading region — electronics value chains are centred there.

questions.question: What happened to world trade between 1950 and 2008?
questions.explanation: GATT tariff cuts, containers and value chains made trade grow faster than output for decades ("hyperglobalization" in the later years). After 2008 the gap closed ("slowbalization").

options.text: It stayed at the same level
It grew faster than world GDP
It grew more slowly than world GDP
It fell steadily because of protectionism

questions.question: Why did world goods trade grow by about 4.6% in 2025 despite new US tariffs?
questions.explanation: Firms rushed imports ahead of tariff hikes, and demand for AI hardware surged. The WTO expected slower growth in 2026 (about 3.9%).

options.text: Oil prices collapsed, making shipping and fuel imports much cheaper
A WTO dispute panel cancelled the US tariffs in early 2025
Most countries cut their own tariffs to zero in response to US tariffs
Importers frontloaded purchases before tariffs, and trade in AI goods boomed

questions.question: Which of these is a TARIFF instrument of trade policy?
questions.explanation: Tariffs are taxes on traded goods: ad valorem (% of value), specific (per unit) or combined. Quotas, standards and VERs are non-tariff measures.

options.text: An import quota of 1 million tonnes
An ad valorem import duty of 10%

questions.question: Which of these are NON-TARIFF barriers? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Non-tariff barriers: quotas, licensing, embargoes, VERs, standards, local-content rules, public procurement preferences, subsidies. Duties of any kind are tariffs.

options.text: A specific duty of $5 per tonne

questions.question: Which WTO principle requires a country to give all WTO members the same treatment it gives its "best" partner?
questions.explanation: MFN = no discrimination between trading partners (exceptions: free trade areas, customs unions, preferences for developing countries). National treatment = no discrimination between imported and domestic goods after entry.

questions.question: Selling goods abroad below their normal home price to win a market is called…
questions.explanation: WTO rules allow anti-dumping duties if dumping injures the domestic industry. Countervailing duties respond to foreign subsidies.

options.text: Subsidizing — it is always allowed by the WTO
Dumping — it can be answered with anti-dumping duties
An embargo — a ban on trade
Transfer pricing — setting internal prices between affiliates of one company

questions.question: What happened to the US IEEPA-based tariffs in February 2026?
questions.explanation: On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled the IEEPA tariffs unlawful. The government used other laws (Sections 122, 232, 301); the average effective rate was about 11% by April 2026 (Yale Budget Lab), versus 2.7% before 2025.

options.text: The administration raised them to 100% on all imports from every trading partner of the United States
A WTO panel approved them as legitimate national-security trade measures
The US Supreme Court struck them down, and the administration switched to other legal tools
Congress approved them, and they became a permanent part of US tariff law

questions.question: What is "disembodied" technology?
questions.explanation: Embodied technology comes inside goods (machines, materials). Disembodied technology is pure knowledge: patents, licences, know-how, software, consulting.

options.text: Technology owned and controlled by the state rather than by firms
Technology built into machines, equipment and materials sold abroad
Outdated technology that has reached the decline stage of its life cycle
Knowledge transferred without equipment — patents, licences, know-how

questions.question: Which are COMMERCIAL forms of international scientific and technical exchange? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Commercial forms are paid: licences, know-how, engineering, franchising, high-tech goods, FDI. Conferences, publications and academic exchanges are non-commercial forms.

questions.question: The large-scale emigration of highly qualified specialists is called…
questions.explanation: Brain drain is a non-commercial channel of technology transfer: the host country gains knowledge, the home country loses it. Brain gain is the same process seen from the receiving side.

questions.question: Which international agreement of 1883 laid the foundation for protecting inventions across countries?
questions.explanation: The Paris Convention (1883) covers patents, trademarks and industrial designs. The Berne Convention (1886) covers copyright; TRIPS (1994) is the WTO's IP agreement.

options.text: The Bretton Woods Agreement on international monetary cooperation
The Berne Convention for the Protection of Literary and Artistic Works
The Paris Convention for the Protection of Industrial Property
The TRIPS Agreement on intellectual property in the WTO

questions.question: How did Japan close its technological gap in the 1950s–1970s?
questions.explanation: Japan bought thousands of licences and adapted them — often cheaper than its own R&D — while limiting FDI. It is the classic case of catch-up through licence trade.

options.text: By banning foreign technology and developing everything with its own R&D
By recruiting large numbers of scientists from the US and Western Europe
By attracting mainly foreign direct investment from American multinationals
By buying foreign licences on a large scale and improving the technologies

questions.question: Which WTO agreement (1994) set minimum global standards for intellectual property protection?
questions.explanation: TRIPS = Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights. GATS covers services, TRIMs covers trade-related investment measures.

questions.question: Put the stages of the technology life cycle in order.
questions.explanation: The life cycle forms an S-curve. A licence is worth most during growth; mature technologies are sold widely or moved abroad.

questions.question: At which stage of the life cycle is a licence usually the MOST expensive?
questions.explanation: At the growth stage the technology is proven and its market expands fast, so buyers pay the most. At maturity it is standard and cheaper; at decline it is almost worthless.

questions.question: According to the life cycle approach, where do MATURE technologies usually move?
questions.explanation: New technologies appear in leaders (US, Japan, Western Europe) and move down a "cascade" to lower-cost countries as they standardize — linked to Vernon's product life cycle and the "flying geese" model.

options.text: Nowhere — mature technologies stay in their home country until they are fully replaced
From developing countries to the US
From leading countries to NICs and then to developing countries

questions.question: Which model describes industries moving step by step from Japan to the Asian tigers and then to China and South-East Asia?
questions.explanation: In Akamatsu's model a leader passes maturing industries to followers, who later pass them on. Textiles moved UK → Japan → Korea → China → Bangladesh and Vietnam.

options.text: The eclectic paradigm of international production (J. Dunning)

questions.question: Which economy was ranked No. 1 in the Global Innovation Index 2026?
questions.explanation: GII 2026 top 5: Switzerland, Sweden, US, South Korea, Singapore. China is 10th — the only middle-income economy in the top 10.

questions.question: What was special about China's R&D spending in 2025?
questions.explanation: China spent 3.93 trn yuan (2.80% of GDP). The highest R&D intensity is in Israel and South Korea (around 5–6% of GDP).

options.text: It reached 2.80% of GDP — above the OECD average for the first time
It reached 5% of GDP — the highest research intensity in the world
It was almost entirely financed by foreign multinationals in China
It fell below 1% of GDP as foreign firms cut their research in China

questions.question: The gap between countries that create new technologies and those that only use old ones is called…
questions.explanation: Achievements of the scientific and technical revolution are concentrated in a few centres (US, EU, Japan, Korea, China), so the gap with the periphery persists. The output gap is a macroeconomic term.

questions.question: Which technologies are associated with the Fourth Industrial Revolution? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The 4th Industrial Revolution (K. Schwab, 2016) fuses digital, physical and biological technologies: AI, IoT, robotics, big data, biotech, quantum. Steam and the telegraph belong to the 1st and 2nd revolutions.

questions.question: Which is the LARGEST channel of international technology transfer?
questions.explanation: MNEs transfer technology to their own foreign affiliates, which keeps control of the know-how. That is why most royalty payments are intra-firm.

options.text: International exhibitions, fairs and trade shows
Students who return home after studying abroad
Free scientific publications and open-access journals

questions.question: A contract under which a contractor builds a complete plant and hands it over ready to operate is called…
questions.explanation: "Turnkey" — the client only has to turn the key. Extended forms are "product in hand" (with staff training) and "market in hand" (with sales support).

questions.question: In franchising, what does the franchisee usually receive?
questions.explanation: Franchising (McDonald's, KFC, hotels) transfers brand, standards, training and know-how for an initial fee plus royalties.

options.text: A low-interest loan from the central bank to open a new business
Full ownership of the franchisor's company and all its trademarks
Only equipment and machines, without any rights to the brand
The right to use a brand and business system in exchange for fees

questions.question: Under an EXCLUSIVE licence, who may use the invention in the agreed territory?
questions.explanation: Simple (non-exclusive) licence: the licensor may also license others. Exclusive: only the licensee uses it in the territory. Full licence: all rights pass to the licensee — close to selling the patent.

options.text: The licensee and any other licensees the licensor chooses
Anyone who pays a fee to the state

questions.question: Periodic payments to the licensor calculated as a percentage of the licensee's sales are called…
questions.explanation: Royalties are paid regularly (e.g., a few percent of net sales). A lump sum is a fixed amount paid once or in instalments; a combined payment = initial fee + royalties.

questions.question: How long does patent protection for an invention usually last?
questions.explanation: TRIPS sets a minimum of 20 years from filing. "Life + 50/70 years" applies to copyright; trademarks can be renewed indefinitely.

questions.question: A licence granted by the state without the patent owner's consent (e.g., for a vital medicine) is…
questions.explanation: TRIPS allows compulsory licensing in emergencies or in the public interest, with payment to the patent holder. A cross-licence is a mutual exchange of licences between two firms.

questions.question: Which group of countries has a positive balance of licence and royalty payments and creates most innovations?
questions.explanation: Leaders are net exporters of technology. Emerging markets mostly import and adapt technology; least developed countries depend on aid and imported equipment.

options.text: Economies in transition such as Kazakhstan, Moldova and Uzbekistan
Technology leaders such as the US, Japan, Germany, Switzerland
Least developed countries such as Chad, Haiti and Nepal
Raw-material exporters such as Saudi Arabia and Nigeria

questions.question: How would you classify China in technological exchange today?
questions.explanation: China still buys foreign technology and chips but leads in EVs, batteries, solar, 5G and drones. It is moving from the "importer-adapter" group toward the leaders.

options.text: The only net exporter of technology in the world, with no technology imports at all
A country that does not take part in technology exchange
Both a major importer and a fast-growing exporter of technology

questions.question: Which of these is a REAL (physical) investment rather than a financial one?
questions.explanation: Real investment creates physical capital (plants, equipment, buildings). Financial investment means buying securities or placing deposits.

options.text: Buying shares on a stock exchange

questions.question: Why does capital move abroad? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Capital seeks returns, markets, resources, cheap labour, risk diversification and lower taxes. Tariff jumping = producing inside a protected market instead of exporting to it.

questions.question: How large were global FDI flows in 2025 (UNCTAD)?
questions.explanation: FDI rose 6% to about $1.6 trn in 2025 after two years of decline, but the top 20 host economies took more than 80% of it.

questions.question: Norway's Government Pension Fund Global, Saudi Arabia's PIF and Singapore's GIC are examples of…
questions.explanation: Sovereign wealth funds are state-owned investors that place national savings (often from oil revenues or reserves) abroad.

questions.question: Pension funds, insurance companies and mutual funds belong to which group of investors?
questions.explanation: Institutional investors collect the savings of many people and invest them professionally — a major source of portfolio flows.

questions.question: What is the difference between loan capital and entrepreneurial capital?
questions.explanation: Loans, credits and bonds bring interest. Direct and portfolio investments in companies bring profit and dividends.

options.text: There is no difference — they are synonyms
Loan capital is long-term; entrepreneurial capital is always short-term
Loan capital is always private; entrepreneurial capital is always public
Loan capital earns interest; entrepreneurial capital earns profit or dividends

questions.question: Which items belong to the FINANCIAL account of the balance of payments (IMF BPM6)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The financial account records direct and portfolio investment, financial derivatives, other investment and reserve assets. Exports and tourism are in the current account.

questions.question: Which share of voting power is the international threshold for foreign DIRECT investment?
questions.explanation: IMF/OECD: 10% or more of votes = lasting interest and control = FDI. Below 10% = portfolio investment. Above 50% = a subsidiary.

questions.question: A Japanese carmaker builds an assembly plant in the US to sell cars to American buyers. What is the main motive (Dunning)?
questions.explanation: Market-seeking FDI serves the host market (often to avoid tariffs). Resource-seeking — raw materials; efficiency-seeking — lower costs; strategic-asset-seeking — buying technology or brands.

questions.question: A chocolate maker buys cocoa plantations abroad. This is…
questions.explanation: Backward vertical FDI goes into earlier stages (inputs); forward vertical FDI — into distribution and sales. Horizontal = the same product abroad. Conglomerate = an unrelated industry.

questions.question: Which are components (financing sources) of FDI flows? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: FDI statistics include new equity, profits that affiliates keep and reinvest, and loans between parent companies and affiliates.

questions.question: Which country was both the largest recipient and the largest source of FDI in 2025?
questions.explanation: The US received about $277 bn. Next hosts: Singapore ($151 bn), Hong Kong ($116 bn), China ($105 bn).

questions.question: Building a new enterprise abroad from scratch is called…
questions.explanation: Greenfield = a new plant. Brownfield = mergers and acquisitions of existing firms (or rebuilding an existing site).

questions.question: Nippon Steel's purchase of US Steel ($13.8 bn, 2025) is an example of…
questions.explanation: Buying control of an existing company abroad is cross-border M&A. It was the largest US deal of 2025.

options.text: A licence agreement (rights to patents and trademarks)

questions.question: A foreign investor owns 35% of a company's voting shares. For the investor, this company is…
questions.explanation: 10–50% = associate; over 50% = subsidiary; a branch is an unincorporated, wholly owned unit; below 10% = portfolio holding.

questions.question: What is the difference between FDI flows and FDI stock?
questions.explanation: Flow = annual movement (water through a pipe). Stock = accumulated position (water in the tank) at the end of the year.

options.text: Flows are only inward investment; stock is only outward investment of a country
Flows include only greenfield projects; stock includes only mergers and acquisitions
Flows are measured in numbers of shares; stock is measured in national currency
Flows are investment made during a year; stock is the accumulated value at a given date

questions.question: Why do large FDI flows pass through the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Ireland?
questions.explanation: Conduit flows via holding companies inflate FDI statistics. The OECD/G20 global minimum tax (15%, from 2024) aims to limit tax-driven structures.

options.text: Their labour costs are the lowest in the whole European Union
MNEs route them through special purpose entities there, often for tax reasons
EU law requires all foreign investment into the EU to be registered through them first
These countries host the largest car and steel factories in Europe

questions.question: Put the FDI waves in chronological order.
questions.explanation: 1870s–1914 → 1950s–1960s → late 1980s → around 2000 → 2024–2026. Each wave followed technological change, liberalization or currency shifts and usually ended with a crisis.

options.text: British investment in railways and mines
Japanese FDI boom driven by the strong yen
US multinationals expand into Western Europe
Global M&A boom and dot-com peak

questions.question: What usually ENDS an FDI growth wave?
questions.explanation: Waves ended with the dot-com crash (2001), the global financial crisis (2008–2009) and COVID-19 (2020). Technology, liberalization and cheap credit start waves.

questions.question: Portfolio investment is…
questions.explanation: Portfolio investment is liquid and fast-moving ("hot money") and gives no management control.

options.text: Receiving an IMF loan to support the balance of payments
Building a new factory abroad and hiring local workers to run it
Buying more than 50% of a foreign company to manage its operations
Buying foreign shares (below 10%) and bonds for income, without control

questions.question: Which factors usually INCREASE portfolio investment into emerging markets? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Investors "search for yield" when rates at home are low. Higher US rates, crises, sanctions and devaluations cause outflows.

options.text: Low interest rates in developed countries
A sharp rise in US interest rates

questions.question: Why is portfolio investment considered riskier for a host country than FDI?
questions.explanation: Shares and bonds can be sold in seconds; factories cannot. Sudden outflows fuelled crises in Asia (1997), Russia (1998) and Argentina (2001).

options.text: It requires building new factories that may stay unused for years
It can leave very quickly ("sudden stops"), triggering currency crises
It always comes with high taxes and fees for the host government
It is banned by IMF rules in most emerging-market economies

questions.question: Which are factors of the globalization of finance? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Deregulation, ICT, floating rates (which created demand for FX trading and hedging), financial innovation, MNEs and institutional investors all globalized finance.

options.text: The introduction of the gold standard

questions.question: How much was traded on the global FX market per day in April 2025 (BIS)?
questions.explanation: $9.6 trn a day (+28% vs 2022). About four days of FX trading equal a whole year of world trade (~$35 trn).

questions.question: The London "Big Bang" of 1986 is an example of…
questions.explanation: The Big Bang abolished fixed commissions and opened the London Stock Exchange to foreign firms, boosting London as a global financial centre.

questions.question: The "Lucas paradox" refers to the fact that…
questions.explanation: Theory predicts that capital should flow to capital-poor countries with higher returns, but large flows go "uphill" — e.g., Asian savings into US assets.

options.text: Capital often flows from emerging economies to rich countries, not the reverse
Rich countries always run trade surpluses with emerging economies
FDI never reaches developing countries without official guarantees
Interest rates are usually higher in developed than in emerging economies

questions.question: What does a US net international investment position of about −$26 trillion (2025) mean?
questions.explanation: NIIP = foreign assets − foreign liabilities. Foreigners hold far more US assets (Treasuries, shares) than Americans hold abroad.

options.text: US foreign liabilities exceed its foreign assets — it is the world's largest net debtor
The US has lent $26 trillion more to other countries than it has borrowed
The US federal budget deficit has reached $26 trillion in a single year
The US central bank holds $26 trillion of gold, foreign currency and other reserve assets

questions.question: For many low- and middle-income countries, which external flow is often LARGER than FDI?
questions.explanation: Remittances are large and stable — for many countries they exceed both FDI and development aid.

questions.question: Which institution is called "the central bank of central banks"?
questions.explanation: The BIS (Basel, 1930) serves central banks and hosts the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision. The World Bank lends for development.

options.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) in Washington

questions.question: What is the main function of the IMF?
questions.explanation: IMF = balance of payments and macro stability. World Bank = development projects. WTO = trade rules.

options.text: Monetary cooperation and loans to countries with balance-of-payments problems
Long-term loans for infrastructure, education and poverty reduction projects
Setting and enforcing the rules of world trade between member countries
Supervising stock exchanges and commercial banks in all member countries

questions.question: Which are participants (subjects) of world finance? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Subjects are actors: states, central banks, international financial institutions, banks, institutional investors, MNEs, exchanges, rating agencies, households. Cycles and balances are phenomena and indicators.

options.text: Rating agencies such as S&P and Moody's

questions.question: Which segment of the financial market deals with instruments maturing in up to one year?
questions.explanation: Money market: interbank loans, Treasury bills, commercial paper (under 1 year). Capital market: long-term bonds and shares.

questions.question: A Japanese company issues dollar bonds in the US market under US rules. These are…
questions.explanation: A foreign bond is issued in another country's market and currency (Yankee — US, Samurai — Japan, Panda — China). A eurobond is issued outside the country of its currency.

questions.question: A eurobond is…
questions.explanation: For example, a dollar bond issued in London is a eurobond. The "euro-" prefix is older than the euro itself (eurodollars since the 1950s–60s).

options.text: A bond denominated in a currency other than that of the country where it is issued
A bond that can be issued only in euros and only inside the euro area
A bond that only citizens and companies of EU member countries are allowed to buy and sell
A bond issued by the European Central Bank to finance EU member states

questions.question: Which country is the largest centre of FX trading?
questions.explanation: London had 37.8% in 2025 (BIS), followed by the US, Singapore (11.8%) and Hong Kong. Its time zone between Asia and America helps.

options.text: The United Kingdom (London) — about 38% of global turnover
Hong Kong (China) — about 45% of global turnover
The United States (New York) — about 70% of global turnover

questions.question: Which were features of the classical gold standard? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Gold also moved freely across borders, and banknotes had to be backed by gold. Gold parities fixed exchange rates within narrow "gold points". Floating rates belong to the Jamaican system; dollar dominance to Bretton Woods.

options.text: Central banks could print money without gold backing
The US dollar was the only reserve currency
Banknotes were freely convertible into gold
Each currency had a fixed gold content

questions.question: Under the gold standard, how was a trade deficit corrected automatically (D. Hume's price–specie flow)?
questions.explanation: Deficit → gold outflow → less money → deflation → cheaper exports → balance restored. The cost of this mechanism was deflation and unemployment.

options.text: The IMF provided a loan → reserves were restored → imports resumed
Gold flowed out → money supply fell → prices fell → exports rose
The government set import quotas → imports fell → the balance improved
The central bank devalued the currency → exports became cheaper

questions.question: Put the world monetary systems in chronological order.
questions.explanation: Paris (1867) recognized gold as world money → Genoa (1922) allowed key currencies as reserves → Bretton Woods (1944) → Jamaica (1976, in force 1978).

questions.question: Which event finally destroyed the gold standard in the 1930s?
questions.explanation: WWI had already suspended convertibility; the Depression caused competitive devaluations and the collapse of the restored gold standard.

options.text: The Great Depression — Britain left gold in 1931 and the US devalued in 1933–1934
The end of World War I and the Treaty of Versailles in 1919
The first oil shock and the OPEC embargo of 1973–1974
The creation of the IMF and the World Bank at the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944

questions.question: At what price was the US dollar convertible into gold under Bretton Woods?
questions.explanation: $35 per ounce from 1934 and under Bretton Woods (1944). $20.67 was the pre-1934 price; $38 came with the Smithsonian Agreement (1971).

questions.question: Within what band could currencies fluctuate around their dollar parity under Bretton Woods?
questions.explanation: ±1% under Bretton Woods; ±2.25% after the Smithsonian Agreement and in the European ERM; ±15% in the ERM after 1993.

questions.question: What is the Triffin dilemma?
questions.explanation: R. Triffin (1960): the reserve-currency country faces a conflict between the world's need for dollars and the credibility of its gold promise. The second option describes the "impossible trinity".

options.text: Capital flows from poor to rich countries
To supply world liquidity the US had to run deficits, which undermined trust in dollar–gold convertibility
Fixed exchange rates, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy cannot all exist at the same time

questions.question: What happened on 15 August 1971?
questions.explanation: The "Nixon shock" ended dollar–gold convertibility. After the Smithsonian Agreement (December 1971) failed, major currencies floated from 1973.

options.text: The Jamaican Agreement demonetized gold and legalized floating exchange rates
The IMF created the SDR as a new international reserve asset
The Smithsonian Agreement raised the official gold price to $38 per ounce and widened the bands
President Nixon closed the "gold window" — the dollar stopped being convertible into gold

questions.question: Which were principles of the Jamaican monetary system? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Agreed in Kingston in January 1976, in force from 1978. Gold lost its official role, the SDR was declared the main reserve asset, floating was legalized, and the IMF began surveillance of exchange-rate policies.

options.text: Compulsory pegs to the US dollar
A gold-backed dollar as the key currency
A fixed parity of $35 per ounce

questions.question: Which currencies make up the SDR basket (since 2016)?
questions.explanation: The yuan joined in October 2016. 2022 weights: USD 43.38%, EUR 29.31%, CNY 12.28%, JPY 7.59%, GBP 7.44%.

options.text: US dollar, euro, Swiss franc, Japanese yen, British pound
US dollar, euro, Chinese yuan, Japanese yen, British pound
US dollar, euro, Chinese yuan, Swiss franc, British pound
US dollar, euro, Chinese yuan, Indian rupee, Japanese yen

questions.question: What share of global foreign-exchange reserves was held in US dollars in Q2 2026 (IMF COFER)?
questions.explanation: 56.7% in dollars, 20.6% in euros. The dollar's share has fallen from about 71% in 2001, but it remains dominant.

questions.question: When did the European Monetary System start?
questions.explanation: The EMS began on 13 March 1979 (initiative of H. Schmidt and V. Giscard d'Estaing). 1957 — Treaty of Rome; 1992 — Maastricht; 1999 — the euro.

questions.question: Which were elements of the European Monetary System? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: The ECB and the euro came later with the Economic and Monetary Union (1998–2002). The ECU was converted into the euro at 1:1 in 1999.

options.text: The ECU — a basket currency unit

questions.question: What happened on "Black Wednesday", 16 September 1992?
questions.explanation: Speculators (e.g., George Soros) bet against the pound. After the crisis the ERM band was widened to ±15% (1993).

options.text: The Bundesbank raised its rate to 20% to stop capital flight
The euro fell below parity with the US dollar for the first time
Greece announced a default on its debt and asked for an EU bailout
The UK (and Italy) were forced out of the ERM by speculative attacks

questions.question: Which is a Maastricht convergence criterion for joining the euro?
questions.explanation: Criteria: inflation ≤ 1.5 p.p. above the three best; deficit ≤ 3% of GDP; debt ≤ 60% of GDP; long-term rates ≤ 2 p.p. above the three best; two years in ERM II without devaluation.

options.text: A budget deficit no higher than 3% of GDP
Unemployment below 5% of the labour force
Real GDP growth above 3% for two years
A trade surplus of at least 2% of GDP

questions.question: How many countries are in the euro area after Bulgaria joined on 1 January 2026?
questions.explanation: Croatia became the 20th member in 2023, Bulgaria the 21st in 2026. EU members outside: Czechia, Denmark, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Sweden.

questions.question: What is the main weakness in the design of the Economic and Monetary Union?
questions.explanation: The ECB sets one interest rate, but budgets stay national. This contributed to the 2010–2012 debt crisis; responses include the ESM, banking union and NextGenerationEU.

options.text: Too many national currencies still circulating in parallel
No central bank to conduct a common monetary policy
A single monetary policy without a common fiscal policy
A fixed exchange rate of the euro to the US dollar

questions.question: Which three ratios make up UNCTAD's Transnationality Index (TNI)?
questions.explanation: The TNI is the average of the three foreign shares. A higher TNI means a more internationalized company.

options.text: Number of host countries, number of affiliates and number of global brands
Exports/GDP, imports/GDP and FDI inflows/gross fixed capital formation of the home country
Foreign assets/total assets, foreign sales/total sales, foreign employment/total employment
Profit/sales, debt/equity and R&D spending/total sales of the firm

questions.question: Put the stages of a firm's internationalization in order.
questions.explanation: The firm moves from exchange to production abroad and finally to a globally integrated system controlled from one centre.

options.text: Running an integrated global network with one strategy (transnational firm)

questions.question: According to OECD estimates, MNEs produce about what share of world GDP?
questions.explanation: MNEs (headquarters plus affiliates) produce about 1/3 of world GDP and more than half of world exports; the output of foreign affiliates ($25.6 trn in 2023) almost equals world trade.

questions.question: Which measure introduced from 2024 targets profit shifting by large MNEs?
questions.explanation: Pillar Two makes large groups pay at least 15% effective tax in each country, reducing the benefit of booking profits in tax havens.

options.text: A 50% withholding tax on all royalties (UN convention)
A global minimum corporate tax of 15% (OECD/G20 Pillar Two)
A ban on foreign subsidiaries in tax havens (WTO rule)
The abolition of double taxation treaties (G7 decision)

questions.question: Who is the author of the eclectic (OLI) paradigm?
questions.explanation: Dunning (University of Reading, 1976–77) combined ownership, location and internalization theories. Vernon — product life cycle; Hymer — monopolistic advantage; Porter — the diamond.

questions.question: According to the OLI paradigm, when should a firm choose FDI?
questions.explanation: O only → licensing; O + I → export; O + I + L → FDI.

options.text: When it has only Ownership advantages
Whenever the host country offers subsidies
When it has Ownership and Internalization advantages but no Location advantage
When it has Ownership, Location and Internalization advantages together

questions.question: A firm has a unique technology (O) and wants to keep it inside the firm (I), but production abroad gives no benefit (no L). What is its best entry mode?
questions.explanation: Without location advantages it is better to produce at home and export. Without internalization advantages the firm would license instead.

questions.question: In the OLI paradigm, which question does each letter answer?
questions.explanation: Ownership = what (unique assets). Location = where (host-country conditions). Internalization = how (inside the firm vs through the market).

options.text: O — who owns the firm; L — how much to invest; I — when to invest
O — what the firm has; L — where to produce; I — how to use the advantage
O — which market; L — which product; I — which currency
O — the firm's country of origin; L — its legal form abroad; I — its income from investment

questions.question: Which of these is an OWNERSHIP advantage (asset type, Oa)?
questions.explanation: Ownership advantages belong to the firm: technology, brands, know-how, management, access to capital. Host-country features are location advantages; transaction costs relate to internalization.

options.text: Low corporate taxes and generous investment incentives in the host country
Cheap labour in the host country
A strong global brand and patented technology

questions.question: Benefits a firm gets from managing a network of affiliates (economies of scale and scope, global sourcing, knowledge sharing) are called…
questions.explanation: Dunning split O into Oa (assets), Ot (common governance of a network) and Oi (institutional — culture, governance, ethics).

options.text: Location advantages of the host country's industrial clusters

questions.question: Why does a foreign firm need ownership advantages at all (S. Hymer)?
questions.explanation: Foreign firms face extra costs (language, law, networks). Only a unique advantage lets them compete with local firms.

options.text: Because host governments allow only foreign firms that own patents to enter
To pay lower taxes at home
To offset the "liability of foreignness" — local firms know the market better

questions.question: Internalization theory is based on which concept?
questions.explanation: When markets for know-how are costly or risky (search, negotiation, leakage), firms "internalize" — they do the activity themselves through FDI.

options.text: The investment multiplier (J. M. Keynes; R. Kahn)
Transaction costs (R. Coase, O. Williamson; Buckley & Casson)
Comparative advantage and factor endowments (D. Ricardo; Heckscher & Ohlin)
Purchasing power parity (G. Cassel; B. Balassa)

questions.question: Which are reasons to INTERNALIZE (choose FDI instead of a licence)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Firms internalize to protect know-how, control quality and avoid search and negotiation costs. High market failures favour internalization. If licensing markets work well, licensing or franchising is enough; without unique assets the firm has nothing to internalize.

options.text: The firm has no unique assets
To control quality and the brand
To make the technology available to as many local firms as possible
Markets for technology work almost perfectly

questions.question: McDonald's mainly uses franchising abroad, while pharmaceutical firms keep R&D and production in-house. Why?
questions.explanation: Where knowledge is easy to protect in contracts, licensing or franchising works; where leakage risk is high, firms internalize.

options.text: Pharmaceutical companies have no ownership advantages to protect
Franchising is prohibited in the pharmaceutical industry by international WTO rules
McDonald's has no brand or know-how that needs any protection
Fast-food know-how is easy to control by contract; drug know-how leaks easily

questions.question: Which of these is a LOCATION advantage?
questions.explanation: Location advantages are host-country features: market size, resources, costs, infrastructure, institutions, taxes, trade barriers. The other options are ownership advantages.

options.text: A large and fast-growing host market

questions.question: Which examples illustrate location advantages? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Apple's brand and Toyota's production system are ownership advantages of the firms, not features of a place.

options.text: Mexico — access to the US market under USMCA ("nearshoring")

questions.question: Foxconn assembles iPhones for Apple under contract. This is an example of…
questions.explanation: Non-equity modes (contract manufacturing, outsourcing, licensing, franchising) let MNEs control value chains without owning the factories.

options.text: A portfolio investment of Apple in Foxconn's shares
A greenfield FDI project of Apple in China and India
A non-equity mode of international production (contract manufacturing)
A joint venture in which Apple and Foxconn share equity, profits and control equally

questions.question: What is "friendshoring"?
questions.explanation: Friendshoring — to allies; nearshoring — to nearby countries; reshoring — back home. All aim at resilience amid geopolitical risks.

options.text: Moving supply chains to politically allied countries
Returning production from abroad to the company's home country and region

questions.question: How do digital MNEs (Alphabet, Meta, Netflix) differ from traditional MNEs?
questions.explanation: Digital firms serve millions of foreign users online with limited FDI, so FDI statistics understate their global reach.

options.text: They sell only to domestic users and do not operate abroad
They are state-owned and expand abroad only with state aid
They reach foreign markets with few physical assets abroad ("asset-light")
They invest mostly in factories, warehouses and heavy equipment in each foreign market

questions.question: What is driving the current (2024–2026) global investment boom?
questions.explanation: Announced greenfield projects in the US reached about $360 bn in 2025, more than half in AI-related sectors (UNCTAD). Privatization drove the 1990s boom.

options.text: The dot-com bubble — internet start-ups and telecom networks
Privatization of state companies in Eastern Europe and Latin America
Shale oil and gas extraction in the US and Canada
Artificial intelligence — data centres, chips and power infrastructure

questions.question: Which factors caused the global FDI boom of the 1990s–2000s? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Liberalization, privatization, ICT, cheap credit for M&A and regional integration (EU single market, NAFTA) fuelled the boom.

options.text: A return to the gold standard
Privatization in Eastern Europe and Latin America
The opening of China and transition economies

questions.question: Bartlett and Ghoshal's "transnational strategy" combines…
questions.explanation: Transnational firms try to be efficient globally, adapt to local markets and share knowledge across their network.

options.text: Global efficiency, local responsiveness and worldwide learning
Global standardization, central control and one product range
Low prices, high market share and state ownership
Export orientation, import substitution and re-exports

questions.question: What is a strategic alliance?
questions.explanation: Alliances can be equity-based (joint ventures, cross-holdings) or non-equity (R&D consortia, cross-licensing, code-sharing). In a merger the firms lose independence.

options.text: A merger of two firms into one new legal company
A long-term cooperation of firms that stay legally independent
A state holding company that controls several firms
A secret agreement of rivals to fix prices and split markets

questions.question: Which are examples of strategic alliances? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A takeover or a merger ends the independence of at least one partner, so it is not an alliance.

options.text: The 1998 merger of Daimler and Chrysler into one company
Nippon Steel's takeover of US Steel

questions.question: Which event best shows how MNE value chains spread shocks around the world?
questions.explanation: When one link of a global chain fails, production stops elsewhere — interdependence created by MNEs.

options.text: The 1982 Mexican default on loans from foreign banks
The 2021 chip shortage that stopped car factories in many countries
The 1992 ERM crisis caused by speculation against the pound
The 1973 OPEC oil embargo imposed by oil-exporting governments

questions.question: Which are possible NEGATIVE effects of MNEs for host countries? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Technology transfer and jobs are positive effects. Governments try to maximize them and limit the negative ones (FDI screening, minimum tax, standards).

options.text: Dependence of the host economy on decisions made abroad

questions.question: Put the phases of the business cycle in order, starting from an expansion.
questions.explanation: After the trough comes recovery and a new expansion. Classical phases: crisis → depression → recovery → boom.

questions.question: What is the output gap?
questions.explanation: A positive gap means the economy overheats (inflation risk); a negative gap means recession (unemployment above the natural rate).

questions.question: Which component of GDP usually swings the MOST during a business cycle?
questions.explanation: Firms cut investment sharply in recessions and boost it in booms; basic consumption is stable.

questions.question: What is the common "rule of thumb" definition of a recession?
questions.explanation: The US NBER uses a broader definition: a significant decline in activity spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months.

options.text: One year of inflation above 10 percent
One quarter of falling stock market prices
Two consecutive months of rising unemployment
Two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP

questions.question: Which are typical features of a recession? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: In a recession output, investment, profits, imports and credit fall; unemployment and bankruptcies rise; inflation usually slows (stagflation is the exception).

questions.question: How do the IMF and the World Bank define a GLOBAL recession?
questions.explanation: By this definition the World Bank counts global recessions in 1975, 1982, 1991, 2009 and 2020.

options.text: A fall in world real GDP per capita
Two quarters of falling stock markets

questions.question: In the Keynesian model of an open economy, equilibrium requires…
questions.explanation: Injections (investment, government spending, exports) must equal leakages (savings, taxes, imports). In a closed economy without the state: S = I.

options.text: X = M (exports must equal imports every year)
I + G + X = S + T + M (injections equal leakages)
T = G (the government budget is always balanced)

questions.question: If aggregate demand exceeds potential output, the economy has…
questions.explanation: Too much demand means overheating and inflation. Demand below potential means a recessionary gap and unemployment.

questions.question: Which cycle lasts about 3–4 years and is linked to inventories?
questions.explanation: Kitchin 3–4 years (inventories); Juglar 7–11 (equipment investment); Kuznets 15–25 (construction, demography); Kondratiev 45–60 (technological revolutions).

questions.question: The Juglar cycle (7–11 years) is driven mainly by…
questions.explanation: Juglar is the "classic" industrial cycle of fixed capital investment.

options.text: Construction of housing and infrastructure linked to demographic waves

questions.question: Put the Kondratiev long waves in order.
questions.explanation: Waves began around the 1780s, 1840s, 1890s, 1940s and 1990s. A 6th wave is expected: AI, biotech, green energy.

questions.question: What is the "political business cycle" (W. Nordhaus)?
questions.explanation: Pre-election stimulus boosts growth and jobs; inflation and fiscal costs show up after the vote.

options.text: Party systems change about every ten years and reset economic policy
Wars and military spending create booms followed by deep slumps
Governments stimulate the economy before elections and tighten after them
Technological revolutions create long waves lasting 45–60 years

questions.question: Which year was NOT a global recession according to the World Bank?
questions.explanation: 2001 was a global slowdown (a US recession after the dot-com crash), but world GDP per capita did not fall. Global recessions: 1975, 1982, 1991, 2009, 2020.

questions.question: Which are common features of the recessions of the last 20 years? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: World trade fell about 12% in 2009; world GDP fell about 3% in 2020. Public debt rose after each crisis.

options.text: Financial or non-economic origin (banks, bubbles, a pandemic)
A return to the gold standard
A massive state response: near-zero rates, quantitative easing, fiscal stimulus

questions.question: Which event turned the US mortgage crisis into a global financial crisis?
questions.explanation: Lehman's bankruptcy froze interbank markets worldwide; in 2009 world GDP fell for the first time since WWII.

options.text: The bankruptcy of the energy trader Enron in December 2001
The Greek debt restructuring in March 2012
The collapse of Lehman Brothers on 15 September 2008

questions.question: What triggered the 1974–1975 recession?
questions.explanation: After October 1973 oil jumped from about $3 to about $12 a barrel. It was the first world recession after WWII.

options.text: The OPEC oil embargo — oil prices rose about four times
A pandemic — lockdowns closed factories and borders
The Lehman collapse — interbank lending froze worldwide
The dot-com crash — technology shares lost most of their value

questions.question: Falling output combined with high inflation, as in 1974–1975, is called…
questions.explanation: Stagflation broke the Phillips-curve logic (inflation vs unemployment) and undermined Keynesian policy, opening the way for monetarism.

questions.question: What were the main causes of the 1980–1982 recession?
questions.explanation: The Iranian revolution (1979) raised oil prices; P. Volcker's Fed raised rates to crush inflation. US unemployment reached 10.8% at the end of 1982.

options.text: German reunification and the crisis of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism
The collapse of the Soviet Union and the end of the CMEA
The second oil shock and very tight US monetary policy (Fed rate near 20%)
The burst of the dot-com bubble and the 9/11 terrorist attacks

questions.question: Which crisis began with Mexico's default in August 1982?
questions.explanation: High US rates and a strong dollar made dollar debts unbearable; the 1980s became a "lost decade" for Latin America.

options.text: The Latin American debt crisis (the "lost decade")

questions.question: Which factors contributed to the 1991–1993 recession? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: German reunification also pushed up European interest rates. The recession was not simultaneous: the US in 1990–1991, Europe in 1992–1993 (plus the ERM crisis); in Japan it started the "lost decade".

options.text: The burst of Japan's asset bubble
The burst of the dot-com bubble

questions.question: Why is the 1991–1993 recession called "unsynchronized"?
questions.explanation: Different shocks (US banks, Japan's bubble, German reunification, ERM tensions) hit regions at different times.

options.text: It hit the US in 1990–1991, but Western Europe mainly in 1992–1993
It lasted only two months in every major economy
It affected only developing countries, not the US or Europe
All major economies entered recession in exactly the same quarter of 1991

questions.question: What was the main cause of the 2001–2003 recession?
questions.explanation: The NASDAQ fell about 78% from March 2000 to October 2002 and IT investment collapsed. 9/11 and corporate scandals (Enron, WorldCom) added to the shock.

options.text: The burst of the dot-com bubble

questions.question: How did the Fed's response to the 2001 recession contribute to the next crisis?
questions.explanation: Cheap money supported the recovery but encouraged mortgage lending and rising house prices — the roots of the 2007–2009 crisis.

options.text: It cut rates to 1% (2003), fuelling the housing bubble behind 2008
It abolished bank capital rules (2003), causing bank runs
It returned the dollar to gold (2002), causing deflation
It raised rates to 20% (2002), causing a Latin American debt crisis

questions.question: How is the unemployment rate calculated?
questions.explanation: Labour force = employed + unemployed people actively looking for work. Students, retirees and discouraged workers are outside the labour force.

questions.question: A programmer loses her job because AI tools automated her tasks, and she needs retraining. This is…
questions.explanation: Structural = a mismatch between skills and jobs. Frictional = between jobs; cyclical = caused by a recession.

questions.question: Natural unemployment is 5%, actual unemployment is 8%, and Okun's coefficient is 2. What is the GDP gap?
questions.explanation: Cyclical unemployment = 8 − 5 = 3 p.p.; × 2 = a 6% output loss. Okun's law (1962): each 1 p.p. of cyclical unemployment ≈ 2–2.5% of lost output.

questions.question: The natural rate of unemployment consists of…
questions.explanation: At "full employment" cyclical unemployment is zero, but frictional and structural unemployment remain (NAIRU).

questions.question: Price increases caused by a sharp rise in energy costs (2022, 2026) are an example of…
questions.explanation: Cost-push inflation comes from the supply side (energy, wages, import prices); demand-pull inflation — from too much spending.

questions.question: Hyperinflation is usually defined (P. Cagan) as price growth of…
questions.explanation: Creeping inflation: up to ~10% a year; galloping: tens to hundreds of percent a year; hyperinflation: over 50% a month (Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008).

questions.question: Which price index uses a FIXED basket of goods from the base period (Laspeyres)?
questions.explanation: CPI = a fixed consumer basket (Laspeyres). The GDP deflator covers all goods produced in the current year (Paasche).

questions.question: What is "core inflation"?
questions.explanation: Central banks watch core inflation to see the underlying trend. The Fed targets 2% PCE inflation, the ECB 2% HICP inflation.

options.text: Inflation of the money supply measured by the growth of M2
Inflation excluding volatile food and energy prices
Inflation measured only in the capital city
Inflation including indirect taxes and fees

questions.question: What does "global transformation of the world economy" mean?
questions.explanation: Directions: industrial → digital economy; a shift of power from the West to Asia; national production → value chains; national → multi-level regulation; energy transition.

options.text: A short-term rise in world GDP during an economic boom across all major economies
A qualitative change of the world economy toward one integrated system
A switch of a country's currency to a new monetary unit
A move of most world production into a single country

questions.question: Which are drivers of global transformation? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Technology, liberalization, MNEs, cheap transport and the end of the Cold War integrated the world. Closed blocs and the gold standard belong to earlier eras.

questions.question: What does the "weaponization of interdependence" mean?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric interdependence gives power to whoever controls key nodes — the dollar system, chips, rare earths.

options.text: Using economic links (sanctions, export controls, SWIFT access) as tools of pressure
Forming military alliances to protect shipping routes, ports and undersea cables worldwide
Banning all foreign trade to become fully self-sufficient
Selling weapons to allies in exchange for trade concessions

questions.question: According to the IMF, what would a closure of the Strait of Hormuz do to world growth in 2026?
questions.explanation: Higher oil prices (around $110 a barrel in the adverse scenario) would spread to every economy — a clear case of global interdependence.

options.text: Cut it by about 0.9 percentage points
Raise it by about 2 percentage points thanks to higher oil revenues

questions.question: Put B. Balassa's stages of economic integration in order.
questions.explanation: An FTA removes internal tariffs; a customs union adds a common external tariff; a common market adds free movement of factors; an EMU adds a single currency and policy coordination.

questions.question: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
questions.explanation: In an FTA each member keeps its own tariffs toward outsiders (so rules of origin are needed). In a customs union they set one external tariff.

options.text: A common external tariff toward non-members
Free movement of labour between members
A common parliament and common courts
A single currency and a common central bank

questions.question: The EU has free movement of goods, services, capital and people, and 21 members use the euro. Which stage is this?
questions.explanation: The EU is a single market; the euro area adds monetary union. Full political union has not been reached.

options.text: A preferential trade agreement (lower tariffs only)
A free trade area (no common external tariff)
Economic and monetary union (for euro members)
Only a customs union (no free movement of factors)

questions.question: According to J. Viner, a regional bloc can reduce welfare when…
questions.explanation: Trade creation: cheaper imports from a member replace dearer home production (good). Trade diversion: cheaper imports from outsiders are replaced by dearer ones from a member (bad).

options.text: Trade creation (cheaper imports from a member) exceeds trade diversion
