Members harmonize product standards and recognize each other's rules
Members remove internal tariffs and quotas on all goods in mutual trade
Trade diversion (imports from a less efficient member) exceeds trade creation

questions.question: Which is the largest free trade area by share of world GDP?
questions.explanation: RCEP (in force since 2022) includes China, Japan, South Korea, ASEAN, Australia and New Zealand — about 30% of world GDP.

questions.question: Which are global problems (they affect all humanity and need joint solutions)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Groups: between societies (war, North–South gap), society and nature (climate, resources, food, water), human and society (demography, health, poverty), new (cyber, AI, debt).

options.text: A rise in one country's VAT rate

questions.question: What is the main UN framework for solving global problems until 2030?
questions.explanation: The SDGs (2015) cover poverty, hunger, health, education, climate, inequality and more.

options.text: The 3 pillars of the Basel III rules
The 10 points of the Washington Consensus

questions.question: When does science become a "direct productive force" in the STR?
questions.explanation: The scientific and technical revolution (from the 1950s) merged science, technology and production; R&D became a sector of its own.

options.text: When universities stop teaching and turn into commercial companies
When scientific knowledge is applied directly in production and creates value
When scientists are moved into factories to work as manual workers
When the state bans private research and runs all laboratories and universities itself

questions.question: How do automation and AI change comparative advantage?
questions.explanation: When robots and AI do routine work, producing near customers becomes cheaper — one reason for reshoring and nearshoring.

options.text: They reduce the importance of cheap labour, encouraging reshoring
They make cheap labour the only factor that matters for where firms locate production

questions.question: Put the stages of the scientific and technical revolution in order.
questions.explanation: 1950s–1970s → 1980s–2000s → today. Each stage changed the structure of the world economy and its innovation leaders.

options.text: Automation, nuclear power, first computers, space
AI, robotics, the Internet of Things, big data

questions.question: Which sector produces the largest share of world output today?
questions.explanation: Services dominate (over 70% in developed countries); industry gives about a quarter, agriculture a few percent.

questions.question: Information, R&D and finance are sometimes grouped into the…
questions.explanation: Primary = raw materials; secondary = industry; tertiary = services; quaternary = knowledge-based services.

questions.question: Which climate milestone did 2024 reach?
questions.explanation: WMO and Copernicus reported about 1.55°C. The Paris Agreement aims to keep long-term warming well below 2°C and pursue 1.5°C.

options.text: It was the first year when all countries reached their net-zero targets
It was the year when global temperatures returned to 1900 levels
It was the first year when global emissions fell below 1990 levels
It was the first calendar year more than 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels

questions.question: What does the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) do?
questions.explanation: CBAM (full phase from 2026) prevents "carbon leakage" — moving dirty production outside the EU's emissions trading system.

options.text: It puts a carbon price on certain imports, such as steel and cement
It pays subsidies to European coal plants to keep energy cheap
It bans imports of all goods from countries without carbon taxes
It sets a single world price for oil and natural gas

questions.question: Which agreement (2015) set the goal of keeping warming well below 2°C?
questions.explanation: Kyoto (1997) set binding targets only for developed countries; Montreal (1987) protects the ozone layer.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four determinants of Porter's "diamond"?
questions.explanation: The four: factor conditions; demand conditions; related and supporting industries; firm strategy, structure and rivalry. Chance and government act from outside.

questions.question: Which economy topped the IMD World Competitiveness Ranking 2026?
questions.explanation: Top 5: Singapore, Hong Kong, Switzerland, Taiwan, UAE; the US is 10th. IMD stresses institutional credibility.

questions.question: According to M. Porter, what is the core of national competitiveness?
questions.explanation: Competitiveness is the ability to raise productivity and living standards sustainably, not simply to cut costs or devalue.

questions.question: Which four factors does the IMD use to measure competitiveness?
questions.explanation: IMD evaluates 70 economies on these four factors (341 criteria), combining statistics with an executive survey.

options.text: Exports, imports, tariff levels, non-tariff barriers
Population size, land area, military power, natural resources and nuclear status
Inflation, unemployment, GDP growth, public debt only
Economic performance, government efficiency, business efficiency, infrastructure

questions.question: About what share of world GDP does the US produce (2025)?
questions.explanation: US GDP ≈ $30.8 trn of ~$115 trn. Together with China (~17%) it produces over 40% of world output.

questions.question: Which are factors of US economic development? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Add technology leadership and top universities, rich resources (shale oil and gas), immigration, entrepreneurial culture, strong institutions and secure geography.

options.text: Deep financial markets and the dollar's reserve role
Very cheap labour compared with Asia

questions.question: What made the US the world's largest oil and gas producer?
questions.explanation: Since the 2010s shale production has made the US a top producer and a major LNG exporter; in 2025 it had a record petroleum trade surplus.

options.text: Nationalization of oil companies (a state monopoly)
New offshore fields in Alaska (Arctic drilling)
The shale revolution (fracking and horizontal drilling)

questions.question: About what share of US GDP is personal consumption?
questions.explanation: The US economy is consumer-driven, which is why its import demand is so large.

questions.question: About what share of US GDP comes from services?
questions.explanation: Services ~80%, industry ~18% (manufacturing ~10%), agriculture ~1% — but US farms are highly productive exporters.

questions.question: Which US region is called the "Rust Belt"?
questions.explanation: The Rust Belt (Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania) lost jobs as heavy industry declined; the Sun Belt (South) attracts new factories and energy projects.

options.text: California's Silicon Valley and the tech West Coast
The financial Northeast around New York and Boston
The Midwest and Great Lakes area of old heavy industry
The oil-rich South, including Texas and Louisiana

questions.question: Which 2022 law supports building chip factories in the US (e.g., TSMC in Arizona)?
questions.explanation: The CHIPS Act subsidizes semiconductor production and R&D to reduce dependence on Asia.

questions.question: How large was US direct investment abroad at the end of 2024 (BEA)?
questions.explanation: The US is the largest source of FDI; most US investment abroad is in Europe (UK, Netherlands, Ireland, Luxembourg), Canada and Asia.

questions.question: Which are features of American TNCs today? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta lead; Nvidia became the first company worth $5 trn (October 2025).

options.text: Value based on intangible assets (IP, brands, data)
Use of low-tax jurisdictions such as Ireland
Dominance of the digital economy and platforms
Activity only in the domestic market

questions.question: What was the US federal budget deficit in fiscal year 2026 (CBO)?
questions.explanation: Debt held by the public reached 100% of GDP — the highest since 1946; net interest costs are about 3.3% of GDP.

questions.question: A large budget deficit combined with a large current-account deficit is called…
questions.explanation: The US has both: a budget deficit of about 6% of GDP and a trade deficit of about $900 bn (2025).

questions.question: Which are current problems of the US economy? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Other risks: a possible AI bubble, dependence on Asian supply chains, slower labour-force growth because of tighter immigration.

questions.question: What was the US goods and services trade balance in 2025?
questions.explanation: Exports $3.43 trn and imports $4.33 trn were both records. Goods deficit $1.24 trn (record); services surplus $339.5 bn (record).

questions.question: In which part of trade does the US run a SURPLUS?
questions.explanation: The US is the world's largest exporter of services; the services surplus partly offsets the huge goods deficit.

options.text: Neither goods nor services (a deficit in both)
Both goods and services (an overall trade surplus)

questions.question: What happened to the US goods deficit with China in 2025?
questions.explanation: Tariffs cut trade in both directions; imports shifted to Mexico, Vietnam, Taiwan and others. Mexico is the largest source of US imports.

options.text: It fell about 32% to around $202 billion
It turned into a US surplus of $50 billion

questions.question: Which statement about Canada is correct?
questions.explanation: Canada (~$2.2 trn GDP) has oil sands, gas, potash, uranium, nickel, gold, aluminium, timber, fresh water and hydropower.

options.text: It is outside all trade agreements, including CUSMA
It is the 2nd-largest country by area and a resource-rich G7 member
It is the most populous country in the Americas and a BRICS member
It has no oil reserves and imports all its energy from the US

questions.question: Where are Canada's main AI research centres?
questions.explanation: Pioneers such as G. Hinton (Toronto) and Y. Bengio (Montreal) made Canada a leader in AI research.

questions.question: How did Canada's economy perform in 2025?
questions.explanation: Exports fell 1.7% (Statistics Canada); Q4 2025 was −0.6% (annualized), followed by a rebound in Q2 2026.

options.text: GDP grew 1.7%, the slowest since 2020, as exports to the US fell
GDP grew 4% thanks to a boom in car exports to Europe
GDP grew 8% thanks to record oil and gas export revenues
GDP fell 10% as US tariffs closed most of Canada's car and steel plants

questions.question: Which are structural problems of the Canadian economy? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Slower population growth after immigration cuts also limits growth.

options.text: Heavy dependence on the US market
Expensive housing and high household debt

questions.question: What share of Canada's merchandise exports went to the US in 2025?
questions.explanation: 71.6% in 2025, down from 75.9% in 2024 — under US tariff pressure Canada started to diversify.

questions.question: Why did about 90% of Canadian exports to the US stay tariff-free in 2025?
questions.explanation: CUSMA-compliant goods were exempt from most new US tariffs; steel, aluminium and some other goods still faced Section 232 duties.

options.text: Canada paid a special fee to the US
The WTO banned US tariffs on Canada
They complied with CUSMA (USMCA) rules of origin
Canada joined the US customs territory and adopted the US external tariff

questions.question: What happened at the CUSMA/USMCA joint review on 1 July 2026?
questions.explanation: Canada and Mexico supported renewal; the US chose bilateral talks. The agreement now expires on 1 July 2036 unless the parties agree to extend it.

options.text: All three countries renewed it for 16 more years, until 2042
The US withdrew, so the agreement ended immediately and tariffs returned on 1 July
The US declined to renew it; annual reviews follow until it expires in 2036
Canada left it and signed a separate free trade deal with the EU

questions.question: Which trade agreements is Canada part of? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Canada uses these deals to diversify away from the US; RCEP and Mercosur do not include Canada.

questions.question: What is Japan's position by nominal GDP after 2025?
questions.explanation: China passed Japan in 2010, Germany in 2023, India in 2025 (IMF data). Japan's GDP is about $4.2 trn.

options.text: 2nd — it is still ahead of China
3rd — it is still ahead of Germany

questions.question: In which industries is Japan a global leader?
questions.explanation: Toyota, Honda, Fanuc, Tokyo Electron and Shin-Etsu show Japan's strength in precision manufacturing and key materials.

options.text: Oil and gas extraction, petrochemicals, coal mining and metal ore production
Coffee, cocoa and other tropical agricultural products
Mass assembly of low-cost clothing and footwear
Cars, robotics, machine tools, chip-making equipment and materials

questions.question: Which country overtook Japan as the world's largest net creditor (end-2024 data, published in 2025)?
questions.explanation: Japan had held first place for 34 years. The US, by contrast, is the largest net debtor.

questions.question: What is the main weakness of Japan's natural resource potential?
questions.explanation: Mountainous islands with few minerals — so Japan specialized in high value-added manufacturing and buys raw materials abroad.

options.text: It exports most of its oil and has to import food
It has too much farmland and too few industrial cities
It depends on neighbours for access to the sea
It imports almost all of its oil, gas, coal and iron ore

questions.question: About what share of Japan's population is aged 65 and over?
questions.explanation: Japan is the oldest major society in the world; its population (~124 million) is shrinking — hence labour shortages and pension pressure.

questions.question: What is the Toyota production system known for?
questions.explanation: Lean methods cut waste and inventories. They spread worldwide and are an ownership advantage of Japanese firms.

options.text: Hand production by craftsmen without assembly lines
Full automation of all plants without any human workers
Mass production with large safety inventories, long runs and a strict hierarchy

questions.question: Put Japan's post-war stages in order.
questions.explanation: 1945–52 → 1955–73 → 1973–85 → 1985–91 → 1991–2012 → 2012–2020. In the 2020s inflation returned and the Bank of Japan began raising rates.

options.text: US occupation and reforms (land reform, breakup of the zaibatsu)

questions.question: What were the "three arrows" of Abenomics?
questions.explanation: PM Shinzo Abe (2012–2020) tried to end deflation; the result was a weak yen and higher stock prices, but modest growth.

options.text: Higher taxes, lower spending and a strong yen to fight inflation
Monetary easing, fiscal stimulus, structural reforms

questions.question: What did the Plaza Accord (1985) do?
questions.explanation: To soften the strong yen's impact, the Bank of Japan cut rates; cheap money inflated share and land prices until the 1990–91 crash.

options.text: It strengthened the dollar and weakened the yen, boosting Japanese exports
It weakened the dollar and strengthened the yen, which later fed Japan's bubble
It opened Japan's rice market to US and Australian farmers
It ended the gold standard and introduced floating exchange rates

questions.question: Which institution steered Japan's industrial policy during the "miracle"?
questions.explanation: MITI directed credit, licences and protection toward priority industries (steel, ships, electronics, cars).

options.text: SCAP (Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers in occupied Japan)
MITI (Ministry of International Trade and Industry)

questions.question: What are keiretsu?
questions.explanation: Keiretsu (e.g., the Mitsubishi and Sumitomo groups) replaced the pre-war zaibatsu; general trading houses (sogo shosha) are another Japanese feature.

options.text: Foreign companies allowed to operate in special zones
General trading houses (sogo shosha) that import raw materials and export finished goods
Groups of companies linked by cross-shareholdings, often around a main bank
State-owned factories created by MITI after the war

questions.question: Which is Japan's largest export industry?
questions.explanation: Cars and parts lead exports, followed by machinery, electronic components and chip-making equipment.

questions.question: About what share of Japan's GDP comes from manufacturing?
questions.explanation: About 20% is high for a developed country (the US has about 10%); services are about 70% of Japan's GDP.

questions.question: Which free trade agreements is Japan part of? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Japan led CPTPP after the US left the TPP in 2017 and signed partnership agreements with the EU (2019) and the UK.

questions.question: Where does most of Japan's external income come from today?
questions.explanation: Since the 1980s Japanese firms have produced abroad (Asia, the US); investment income now exceeds the trade balance.

options.text: Foreign aid received from the US and the EU
A large trade surplus in cars and electronics, as in the 1980s
Income on foreign investments rather than the trade surplus
Tourism receipts rather than trade or investment

questions.question: What was the core of the 2025 US–Japan trade deal?
questions.explanation: The deal avoided higher threatened tariffs; Japan pledged to invest in strategic US industries.

options.text: Japan joining USMCA as a fourth member from 2026
A ban on Japanese car exports to the US until 2030
A 15% US tariff in exchange for Japanese investment pledges in the US
Full free trade with zero tariffs on all goods in both directions

questions.question: What did the Bank of Japan do in December 2025?
questions.explanation: The BoJ ended negative rates in 2024 and continues gradual normalization because inflation has stayed above 2%.

options.text: It raised its policy rate to 0.75%, a 30-year high
It started a new round of negative rates to weaken the yen

questions.question: Which are current problems of Japan's economy? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Others: low productivity in services, a weak yen, US tariffs. PM Sanae Takaichi (since October 2025) adopted a ¥21.3 trn stimulus.

options.text: The highest public debt among developed countries

questions.question: How fast did Japan's GDP grow in 2025?
questions.explanation: After −0.2% in 2024. Potential growth is well below 1% because of demography.

questions.question: Where does Germany rank among the world's largest economies?
questions.explanation: GDP is about $5 trn; Germany is the largest economy in the EU (about a quarter of EU GDP).

questions.question: What happened to Germany's GDP in 2023–2025?
questions.explanation: −0.9% (2023), −0.5% (2024), +0.2% (2025) — the longest stagnation in post-war history (Destatis).

options.text: It grew 5% in 2024, then fell 1% in 2025
It grew about 3% each year thanks to exports
It fell by 10% in 2025 after a new energy crisis
It fell in 2023 and 2024 and grew only 0.2% in 2025

questions.question: Which pair of countries is called the "engine" of European integration?
questions.explanation: Franco-German cooperation drove the ECSC, the euro and many EU reforms.

questions.question: What is the German "Mittelstand"?
questions.explanation: "Hidden champions" dominate world niches (machines, components) — a key source of German export strength.

options.text: The group of eastern German regions that joined in 1990
The federal central bank that manages German monetary policy
A national federation of trade unions in the metal industry
Thousands of family-owned SMEs, many of them global niche leaders

questions.question: Which German institution combines school with training in a company?
questions.explanation: Dual training produces the highly skilled workforce that German industry relies on.

questions.question: Who is associated with the concept of the German "social market economy"?
questions.explanation: Erhard (economy minister 1949–63) combined free markets with social protection; the "economic miracle" followed.

questions.question: About what share of Germany's GDP comes from manufacturing?
questions.explanation: One of the highest shares among developed countries. Key branches: cars, machinery, electrical engineering, chemicals.

questions.question: Which are leading German industrial companies? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Also Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Bosch, BASF, Bayer and SAP (software). Renault is French, Nokia is Finnish, Toyota is Japanese.

questions.question: Which are main problems of the German economy? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Also underinvestment, bureaucracy and slow digitalization; goods exports fell in 2025 because of US tariffs and Chinese competition.

options.text: Shortage of skilled workers due to ageing
Pressure on the car industry from EVs and Chinese rivals
No access to the EU single market
Loss of cheap Russian gas and high energy prices

questions.question: How did Germany change its fiscal rules in 2025?
questions.explanation: Chancellor Friedrich Merz is betting on public investment to restart growth after two years of recession.

options.text: It left the euro area to regain control over its own monetary policy
It abolished corporate taxes to keep car makers from moving to the US
It adopted a strict balanced-budget rule for the first time in its history
It relaxed the debt brake: defence above 1% of GDP is exempt, plus a €500 bn fund

questions.question: About what share of GDP do German exports make up?
questions.explanation: Germany's model is export-led (cars, machinery, chemicals, pharmaceuticals). The US export quota is only about 11%.

questions.question: What does Germany's 2023 China Strategy aim for?

About 7th in the world and 2nd in the euro area

About 20th in the world and 5th in the euro area

Very high public spending — well above half of GDP
Minimal social protection and private pensions only
Very low taxes — well below a quarter of GDP

Deficit 10% of GDP, debt 200% of GDP

questions.question: Why does France oppose the EU–Mercosur trade agreement?

Because the agreement would force France to leave the EU Common Agricultural Policy
To protect its farmers from cheaper South American imports

questions.question: What is France's investment programme for reindustrialization (nuclear, hydrogen, chips) called?

A military coup and the suspension of the constitution of the Fifth Republic
A fragmented parliament and several government collapses
A decision to leave the European Union

questions.question: When did the UK formally leave the European Union?
questions.explanation: 1973 — joined; 2016 — referendum; 31 January 2020 — exit; since 1 January 2021 trade follows the Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

questions.explanation: Zero tariffs apply if rules of origin are met, but border bureaucracy raised trade costs, especially for small firms.

No tariffs or quotas on goods, but new customs and regulatory checks
Full membership in the EU single market and the customs union, as before Brexit
Use of the euro and membership in the ECB system

It is the world's largest oil port and refining hub

questions.question: Which UK industries are internationally strong? Select all that apply.

A lack of universities and a poorly educated workforce
Hyperinflation above 50% a month since Brexit
Weak productivity growth since 2008 and low investment

questions.question: About what share of the UK economy is services?

questions.explanation: The EU as a bloc is bigger (about 40% of trade), but the US is the largest single country, followed by Germany, the Netherlands, Ireland, France and China.

A coast–mountain divide between tourist coasts and the Alps
A capital–provinces divide between Rome and all the other regions of the country

A private car company that later became part of Fiat
The Italian stock exchange in Milan before it was privatized in the 1990s

A bonus paid to exporters who sell outside the EU
A special tax on luxury goods such as jewellery and cars

A plan to leave the euro, return to the lira and devalue it to boost exports

A national space programme with ESA and NASA

questions.question: Which factors explain China's fast growth? Select all that apply.

questions.question: About what share of China's GDP goes to investment?

"Shock therapy" — all market reforms launched at once, as in Russia in 1992

options.text: Electric vehicles, lithium-ion batteries, solar panels

They adopted the US dollar as their only currency from the start

options.text: A strong "developmental state" with industrial policy

options.text: Heavy and chemical industry: steel, ships, petrochemicals

options.text: 8.63% — the fastest in 15 years, driven by AI chips
1.0% — slowed by weak global chip demand
4.6% — in line with world trade growth and the average of Asian economies
−2.0% — hit by new US tariffs on chips

questions.question: Which crisis forced South Korea to ask the IMF for a large rescue package?
questions.explanation: Afterwards Korea restructured its chaebol and banks and recovered quickly.

Closing the economy to all foreign trade and investment

Relying mainly on foreign aid instead of trade
